events.title: Death of Theodosius I and division of the empire
events.summary: Theodosius I died at Milan on 17 January 395, leaving the East to Arcadius (about 17) and the West to Honorius (10). It was meant as a collegiate division within one empire, but the two courts never again had a single ruler with real power over both.
events.detail: Nothing in 395 was formally partitioned: law was still issued in the joint names of both Augusti, consuls were shared, and contemporaries spoke of one res publica. The real fault lines were human and fiscal. Stilicho, magister militum and husband of Theodosius's niece Serena, claimed that the dying emperor had entrusted both sons to him, a claim the eastern court under the praetorian prefect Rufinus rejected. The dispute over the prefecture of Illyricum (the dioceses of Dacia and Macedonia, prime recruiting ground) poisoned relations for fifteen years and gave Alaric room to play one court against the other. The West inherited the longer and more exposed frontiers and a smaller, more aristocratically captured tax base; the East had Egypt's grain and a defensible capital.
events.debate: Whether 395 was a 'division' at all is a modern framing. Kaldellis stresses continuity of a single Roman polity; Heather and others see 395 as the start of diverging fiscal-military systems. Stilicho's claim to guardianship of Arcadius rests on Claudian, his court poet.
scholarship: Cameron & Long, Barbarians and Politics at the Court of Arcadius (1993)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)

events.title: Alaric's Goths revolt and ravage the Balkans and Greece
events.summary: The Gothic federates who had bled at the Frigidus (394) rose under Alaric, marched to the walls of Constantinople, then turned into Thessaly and Greece, sacking Corinth, Argos and Sparta in 395-396. Athens was spared, probably by payment.
events.detail: Alaric's grievance was status and pay: he wanted a regular Roman command, not to lead expendable auxiliaries. Stilicho marched east with the combined army of both halves but was ordered by Arcadius to send the eastern units home; under Gainas they returned to Constantinople and murdered Rufinus. Zosimus's lurid account of the Greek devastation, with Christian monks opening Thermopylae, reflects pagan polemic. Eleusis was destroyed and the Mysteries ended in this period.
events.debate: Whether Alaric was already 'king of the Visigoths' in 395 is doubtful; Kulikowski and Heather see the Gothic people being forged in these years around his leadership rather than pre-existing.

events.title: Murder of the prefect Rufinus at the Hebdomon
events.summary: Gainas's returning eastern troops, saluting Arcadius at the Hebdomon parade ground outside Constantinople, surrounded and hacked to death the praetorian prefect Rufinus; his head and right hand were paraded through the city.
events.detail: Claudian, writing for Stilicho, makes Rufinus a monster; it is likely Stilicho arranged the killing. The beneficiary was not Stilicho but the eunuch grand chamberlain Eutropius, who now dominated Arcadius.

events.title: Stilicho traps Alaric at Pholoe
events.summary: Stilicho landed at Corinth and hemmed Alaric's Goths in on the Pholoe plateau in Elis, but Alaric slipped away to Epirus. Eutropius had the eastern senate declare Stilicho a public enemy, and soon gave Alaric an eastern command in Illyricum.

battle.significance: Showed the cost of the two courts' rivalry: Stilicho was ordered off eastern soil and Alaric was rewarded with the magisterium per Illyricum, the official post he would seek ever after.

events.debate: Zosimus says Stilicho let Alaric escape through negligence and debauchery; Claudian implies a political deal or eastern interference. Modern views lean to the latter.

events.title: Battle of the Ardalio: fall of Gildo
events.summary: Gildo, the Moorish comes Africae who had transferred Africa's allegiance to Constantinople and stopped the grain to Rome, was routed between Theveste and Ammaedara by his own brother Mascezel, sent by Stilicho with about 5,000 veterans. Gildo fled and killed himself at Thabraca.
events.detail: Gildo had murdered Mascezel's sons, so Stilicho chose an avenger. The Senate formally declared Gildo hostis publicus, a revival of republican procedure that Claudian celebrates in De Bello Gildonico. Gildo's vast estates were confiscated into a special treasury, the comitiva Gildoniaci patrimonii, still in the Notitia Dignitatum. Mascezel himself drowned soon afterward; Zosimus claims Stilicho's guards pushed him off a bridge.
events.locName: River Ardalio, between Theveste and Ammaedara

battle.significance: Restored the African grain supply to Rome and the West's control of its richest provinces for another generation.

events.debate: Orosius frames the victory as a miracle after Mascezel prayed at Capraria with monks; numbers are hagiographical.

events.title: Consulship and fall of the eunuch Eutropius
events.summary: Eutropius, Arcadius's grand chamberlain and a former slave, became the first eunuch consul in 399, to western outrage; Claudian's In Eutropium is pure venom. By August the revolt of Tribigild in Phrygia and Gainas's pressure forced his dismissal; he took sanctuary in Hagia Sophia, was exiled to Cyprus and executed at Chalcedon.
events.debate: The West refused to recognise his consulship; the fasti show divergence. Chrysostom preached over the cowering Eutropius in the cathedral.

events.title: Massacre of Gainas's Goths in Constantinople
events.summary: After months in which the Gothic general Gainas dominated the capital, the citizens rose on 12 July 400 while he was outside the walls and slaughtered his Gothic troops, reportedly about 7,000, many burned alive in a church near the palace where they had fled.
events.detail: The episode inspired Synesius's allegory De Providentia and fed the long modern argument over an 'anti-German' party at the eastern court. Cameron and Long dismantled the idea of a coherent ideological faction; the massacre was opportunistic urban violence against a resented garrison.

battle.significance: Ended the threat of a barbarian generalissimo controlling the eastern court.

scholarship: Cameron & Long, Barbarians and Politics at the Court of Arcadius (1993)

events.title: Fravitta destroys Gainas's rafts on the Hellespont
events.summary: Trying to cross from the Thracian Chersonese to Asia on improvised rafts, Gainas's army was shattered by the Liburnian galleys of Fravitta, a pagan Goth loyal to Rome. Gainas fled north of the Danube, where the Hun Uldin killed him and sent his head to Constantinople (arrived 3 January 401).

sides.strength: fleet of Liburnian galleys under Fravitta

battle.significance: First appearance of a Hunnic ruler, Uldin, acting as a diplomatic partner of Constantinople.

events.title: Alaric invades Italy
events.summary: Displaced from his Illyrian command after the fall of Eutropius, Alaric crossed the Julian Alps in November 401 while Stilicho was fighting Vandals and Alans in Raetia. He besieged Aquileia and threatened Milan, where Honorius was cut off until Stilicho returned with troops stripped from the Rhine and Britain.

events.title: Battle of Pollentia
events.summary: On Easter Sunday 402 Stilicho attacked Alaric's camp at Pollentia in Liguria, gambling that the Christian Goths would not expect battle on the feast. The fight was bloody and inconclusive, but Alaric's camp, treasure, wife and children were captured, forcing him to negotiate.
events.detail: Stilicho's Alan contingent under Saul opened the attack and suffered heavily; Saul was killed. Claudian claims a crushing victory; Orosius, writing after Stilicho's disgrace, condemns the sacrilege of fighting on Easter and says the Goths won the fight. Alaric withdrew toward the Po valley under a truce, which he soon broke.

sides.strength: western field army with Alan federates; perhaps 15,000-20,000

battle.significance: A tactical draw but strategic success: Alaric lost his baggage and hostages, and his army began to fray.

events.debate: Claudian (pro-Stilicho) and Orosius (anti-Stilicho) give opposite verdicts; Jordanes's Gothic victory is late and derivative.

events.title: Battle of Verona
events.summary: When Alaric broke the Pollentia truce and moved on Raetia or Gaul, Stilicho caught him near Verona and defeated him; desertions followed and Alaric withdrew to the Balkans with a much reduced following. Stilicho let him go, apparently wanting him as an ally against the East.

battle.significance: Ended Alaric's first invasion of Italy; Honorius celebrated a triumph in Rome in 404, the last imperial triumph held in the old capital.

events.debate: The year is disputed between summer 402 and 403.

events.title: The western court moves to Ravenna
events.summary: Shaken by the siege of Milan, Honorius moved the court to Ravenna around the end of 402. Protected by marshes and with the fleet base at Classis giving access to the Adriatic and Constantinople, Ravenna remained the western capital until 476 and the seat of Odoacer, Theodoric and the exarchs.
events.debate: The move was gradual; Milan remained important and the date of the formal transfer is debated (402-408).

events.title: Second exile of John Chrysostom
events.summary: Deposed by the Synod of the Oak (403) under Theophilus of Alexandria, recalled after an earthquake frightened the empress Eudoxia, then exiled again in June 404 after sermons read as attacks on her silver statue, John Chrysostom left Constantinople. That night Hagia Sophia and the senate house burned. He died on a forced march at Comana in 407.

sources.w: Dialogue on the Life of John Chrysostom

events.debate: The famous 'Herodias' sermon attributed to John may be spurious; the conflict was as much about episcopal jurisdiction and Alexandrian rivalry as about the empress.

events.title: Radagaisus invades Italy
events.summary: A large Gothic-led force under the pagan king Radagaisus crossed the Alps from the middle Danube in late 405 and spread through northern Italy, one of several shock waves set off by Hunnic expansion west of the Carpathians.
events.debate: Zosimus's 400,000 and Orosius's 200,000 are fantasies; Heather suggests 20,000 warriors with families. Heather links Radagaisus, the Rhine crossing and later Hunnic movements as a single migration crisis; Halsall downplays external pressure.

events.title: Battle of Faesulae: destruction of Radagaisus
events.summary: Radagaisus besieged Florence; Stilicho, with 30 numeri plus Uldin's Huns and Sarus's Goths, relieved the city and blockaded the invaders on the heights of Faesulae until hunger broke them. Radagaisus was executed on 23 August 406; 12,000 of his best men were enrolled in the Roman army and so many captives were sold that slaves went for a solidus a head.

sides.strength: 30 numeri (Zosimus), plus Hunnic and Gothic auxiliaries

sides.losses: army surrendered; 12,000 drafted, the rest enslaved

battle.significance: Stilicho's last great victory. The 12,000 recruits later joined Alaric after Stilicho's fall, swelling the force that sacked Rome.

events.debate: Augustine and Orosius use the pagan Radagaisus's defeat to answer claims that Christianity weakened Rome.

events.title: Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Rhine
events.summary: On the last day of 406 (per Prosper) Hasding and Siling Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Rhine near Mainz after defeating Frankish federates who killed the Hasding king Godigisel. For three years they plundered Gaul, then in 409 crossed into Spain; the Hasdings under Gaiseric would end in Carthage.
events.detail: Jerome's letter 123 lists the victims: Mainz sacked and thousands massacred in the church, Worms destroyed, Reims, Amiens, Arras, Tournai, Speyer and Strasbourg taken. The Rhine frontier had been thinned by Stilicho's withdrawals to fight Alaric and Radagaisus. The crisis also triggered the British army's proclamation of Constantine III. The image of a frozen Rhine is a modern embellishment not found in the sources.
events.debate: Kulikowski argued for 31 December 405, reading Zosimus's chronology against Prosper; most still prefer 406. Whether the invaders were pushed by the Huns (Heather) or drawn by opportunity and Roman politics (Halsall, Goffart) is central to the 'fall vs transformation' debate.
scholarship: Kulikowski, 'Barbarians in Gaul, usurpers in Britain', Britannia 31 (2000)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West 376-568 (2007)

events.title: Constantine III proclaimed in Britain
events.summary: After the brief usurpers Marcus and Gratian were murdered, the British garrison proclaimed a common soldier named Constantine, chosen for his name. He crossed to Gaul in 407, took over the Rhine army and the Gallic prefecture, made Arles his capital and extended his rule into Spain.

events.title: Death of Arcadius; accession of Theodosius II
events.summary: Arcadius died on 1 May 408 aged about 31, leaving his seven-year-old son Theodosius II, already Augustus since 402. Real power lay with the praetorian prefect Anthemius, who negotiated peace with Persia and began the great land walls.
events.debate: Procopius's story that Arcadius named the Persian king Yazdegerd I guardian of his son is doubted but not impossible; Agathias already found it suspect.

events.title: Execution of Stilicho
events.summary: After a mutiny at Ticinum on 13 August 408, engineered by the court official Olympius, slaughtered Stilicho's senior officials, Stilicho surrendered from sanctuary at Ravenna and was beheaded on 22 August. Roman troops then massacred the families of barbarian federates across Italy, driving perhaps 30,000 soldiers to join Alaric.
events.detail: The charge was that Stilicho planned to put his son Eucherius on the eastern throne after Arcadius's death and was in league with Alaric. Stilicho refused to let his own barbarian bucellarii fight for him, perhaps the most consequential act of loyalty in late Roman history. Eucherius was killed soon after; Serena was strangled at Rome during Alaric's siege by order of the Senate with Galla Placidia's consent. With Stilicho gone, the West lost its one commander able to manage Alaric, and Olympius's anti-barbarian policy destroyed the military capital Stilicho had built.
events.debate: Zosimus (following Olympiodorus) is sympathetic; Orosius and Rutilius Namatianus, who accused Stilicho of burning the Sibylline Books, hostile. Modern estimates of how many federates defected depend wholly on Zosimus's 30,000.
scholarship: Hughes, Stilicho: The Vandal Who Saved Rome (2010)
Matthews, Western Aristocracies and Imperial Court AD 364-425 (1975)

events.title: Alaric's first siege of Rome
events.summary: In autumn 408 Alaric blockaded Rome and cut the Tiber supply from Portus. Famine and plague followed. The Senate bought him off with 5,000 lbs of gold, 30,000 lbs of silver, 4,000 silk tunics, 3,000 scarlet hides and 3,000 lbs of pepper, partly by melting down statues of the gods.
events.detail: During the siege the urban prefect Pompeianus entertained Etruscan haruspices who offered to call down lightning on the Goths; Pope Innocent reportedly allowed private rites, though the Senate dared not perform them publicly (Zosimus). The ransom list is a precious snapshot of the commodities of a late Roman aristocratic economy.

sides.losses: many dead of famine and disease

sides.strength: Alaric's Goths swollen by Stilicho's former federates and fugitive slaves

battle.significance: Showed that Ravenna would not defend Rome; Alaric used the city as a hostage to extract a settlement from Honorius.

events.title: Second siege of Rome and the elevation of Priscus Attalus
events.summary: After Honorius rejected Alaric's demands at Ariminum (first gold, grain and the Venetian and Noric provinces, then only Noricum), Alaric again blockaded Rome in late 409. The Senate proclaimed the urban prefect Priscus Attalus emperor, who named Alaric magister utriusque militiae and his brother-in-law Athaulf comes domesticorum.
events.detail: Attalus, a pagan baptised by an Arian bishop, failed to secure Africa, whose comes Heraclian stayed loyal to Honorius and cut the grain. Alaric deposed him near Ariminum in summer 410. Honorius had been about to flee to Constantinople when 4,000 eastern troops arrived at Ravenna.

battle.significance: Produced the only Senate-made emperor of the period, a puppet whose failure showed that Rome without Africa could not stand.

events.title: Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Pyrenees
events.summary: In late September or October 409 the Rhine invaders crossed into Spain, apparently admitted by Gerontius, Constantine III's general, who had rebelled and set up his own emperor Maximus. In 411 they divided the provinces by lot: Hasdings and Suebi in Gallaecia, Alans in Lusitania and Carthaginiensis, Silings in Baetica.
events.debate: Hydatius gives 28 September or 13 October; his apocalyptic picture of famine, cannibalism and plague is rhetorical but rooted in local experience. The 411 'lot' may reflect a treaty with Maximus.

events.title: Sack of Rome by Alaric
events.summary: On 24 August 410 Alaric's Goths entered Rome by the Salarian Gate and sacked the city for three days, the first fall of Rome to a foreign enemy since the Gauls c. 390 BC. The basilicas of Peter and Paul were respected as sanctuaries; Galla Placidia, Honorius's sister, was carried off.
events.detail: Militarily the sack changed little: Honorius in Ravenna reportedly confused news of Rome's loss with the death of his pet chicken named Roma (Procopius, a story already told as a joke). Its ideological shock was enormous. Jerome in Bethlehem wrote that 'the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken' (Ep. 127.12). Pagans blamed the abandonment of the gods; Augustine began De Civitate Dei (413-426) in reply and commissioned Orosius's Histories. Damage was limited: the Gardens of Sallust burned, and the Basilica Aemilia's burnt coins fused into its floor have been linked to 410. Alaric left after three days with Placidia and treasure, heading for Africa.

sides.strength: no field army; city walls held by civilians
sides.losses: unknown; probably low by the standards of sacks

battle.significance: No strategic consequence in itself, but a symbolic catastrophe that reshaped Christian historiography and political theology.

events.debate: Procopius's tale of a treacherous gate opening by Proba's slaves or by a Gothic 'gift' of youths is legendary. Ward-Perkins uses 410 and its aftermath as evidence of real violence; Goffart and Halsall stress its limited material impact.
scholarship: Lipps, Machado & von Rummel (eds.), The Sack of Rome in 410 AD (2013)
Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization (2005)

events.title: End of Roman rule in Britain
events.summary: Zosimus records that around 409 the Britons, abandoned by Constantine III and harried by Saxons, expelled Roman officials and defended themselves; and that in 410 Honorius wrote to the cities telling them to look to their own defence. No Roman administration returned.
events.detail: The archaeology is stark: coin supply ended c. 402, villas, towns and pottery industries collapsed within a generation, and Britain saw a sharper material simplification than any other western province. The 'Rescript of Honorius' is problematic: Zosimus places it among Italian events, and some scholars read 'Brettia' as Bruttium in southern Italy.
events.debate: The Bruttium emendation, and whether the 409 'revolt' was a Bagaudic-style social upheaval (Thompson) or a loyalist defence, remain contested. Esmonde Cleary sees systemic collapse already under way before 410.
scholarship: Esmonde Cleary, The Ending of Roman Britain (1989)

events.title: Death and river burial of Alaric
events.summary: Alaric marched to Rhegium intending to cross to Sicily and Africa, but a storm wrecked his ships. He died near Consentia late in 410; Jordanes says his men diverted the river Busentus, buried him and his treasure in the bed, let the waters return and killed the labourers. His brother-in-law Athaulf succeeded.
events.debate: The burial story comes only from Jordanes, who drew on Cassiodorus's lost Gothic History and wrote 140 years later; treasure hunters still dig at Cosenza.

events.title: Siege of Arles and fall of Constantine III
events.summary: Honorius's new general Constantius (the future Constantius III) and Ulfilas besieged Constantine III in Arles, after Gerontius's own siege collapsed. They defeated a relief army under Edobich by an ambush across the Rhône, and Constantine surrendered after being ordained a priest; he was beheaded on the road to Ravenna in September 411.

sides.strength: garrison of Arles; relief army of Franks and Alamanni under Edobich

battle.significance: Restored Ravenna's authority in southern Gaul and launched Constantius's career as the West's strongman.

events.title: Construction of the Theodosian Land Walls
events.summary: Under the regent Anthemius, praetorian prefect of the East, a new land wall was completed by 413 about 1.5 km west of Constantine's, enclosing a much larger city. Running c. 5.7 km from the Propontis to the Golden Horn with 96 towers, it was the core of the defences that held Constantinople until 1453.
scholarship: Van Millingen, Byzantine Constantinople: The Walls of the City (1899)
Crow, 'The infrastructure of a great city', in Lavan et al. (eds.), Technology in Transition (2007)
events.debate: The outer wall and moat date to the reconstruction of 447; the 413 work was the inner wall.

events.title: Athaulf marries Galla Placidia at Narbonne
events.summary: In January 414, in the house of the Narbonne notable Ingenuus, the Gothic king Athaulf married his captive Galla Placidia in Roman dress, with Priscus Attalus singing the epithalamium. Their son, named Theodosius, died in infancy at Barcelona.
events.detail: Orosius reports that a Narbonne citizen heard Athaulf say at Bethlehem that he had once wanted to turn Romania into Gothia, but had decided to use Gothic strength to restore the Roman name, since Goths could not obey laws. Whether authentic or Orosian invention, it is the clearest ancient statement of a barbarian king's aspiration to Roman legitimacy.

events.title: Murder of Hypatia
events.summary: In March 415 a Christian mob led by a lector named Peter dragged the Neoplatonist philosopher and mathematician Hypatia from her carriage in Alexandria, killed her in the Caesareum church, flayed her with potsherds and burned her remains. She had been an adviser to the prefect Orestes in his feud with Bishop Cyril.
events.debate: Socrates, a moderate Christian, condemns the murder as shaming Cyril; John of Nikiu, centuries later, celebrates it. The modern image of Hypatia as a young martyr of science owes much to Gibbon and Kingsley; she was probably about 60.

events.title: Wallia's treaty: Placidia returned for grain
events.summary: Starved by Constantius's naval blockade of the Mediterranean coast, the Goths in Spain under their new king Wallia made peace in 416: they returned Galla Placidia, received 600,000 modii of grain, and agreed to fight the Vandals and Alans in Spain on Rome's behalf.

events.title: Visigoths destroy the Siling Vandals and Alans
events.summary: Fighting as Roman federates, Wallia's Goths annihilated the Siling Vandals in Baetica (their king Fredbal was sent to Honorius) and so mauled the Alans that their king Addac fell; the survivors placed themselves under the Hasding king Gunderic, whence the later royal title 'king of the Vandals and Alans'.

events.title: Visigoths settled in Aquitaine
events.summary: Recalled from Spain by Constantius in 418, Wallia's Goths were settled in Aquitania Secunda and adjoining parts of Novempopulana and Narbonensis, with Toulouse as their centre. Wallia died soon after and was succeeded by Theodoric I. This is conventionally the birth of the Visigothic kingdom.
events.detail: The terms are lost. The legal mechanism, hospitalitas, has been fought over for decades: the traditional view is that Goths received a share (two-thirds?) of estates; Goffart argued they received shares of tax revenue rather than land; Liebeschuetz and Halsall offer intermediate models. Why Aquitaine, a rich interior region, rather than a frontier, is also debated: to guard against Bagaudae and Saxon raiders, or because the Goths could be fed there. The settlement was intended as a Roman military deployment, not a cession of sovereignty.
events.debate: Goffart's fiscal reading of hospitalitas versus land allotment is the classic dispute. Prosper's date is 419; most accept 418.
scholarship: Goffart, Barbarians and Romans AD 418-584: The Techniques of Accommodation (1980)

events.title: Honorius establishes the Council of the Seven Provinces
events.summary: An edict of 17 April 418 to the prefect Agricola ordered an annual assembly of the provincial notables and officials of the Seven Provinces of southern Gaul at Arles between 13 August and 13 September, an attempt to bind the Gallic aristocracy to Ravenna at the moment the Goths were settled among them.

events.title: Imperial condemnation of Pelagianism
events.summary: Lobbied by the African bishops led by Augustine, Honorius issued a rescript on 30 April 418 expelling Pelagius and Caelestius from Rome; the Council of Carthage on 1 May condemned the doctrine that humans can avoid sin without grace. Pope Zosimus, who had exonerated Pelagius, reversed himself in his Epistula tractoria.

events.title: Constantius III made co-emperor
events.summary: Constantius, married to Galla Placidia since 1 January 417 and father of Valentinian (born 2 July 419), was raised to Augustus on 8 February 421; Constantinople refused to recognise him. He died on 2 September 421, complaining that the purple had cost him his freedom.

events.title: Theodosius II marries Athenais-Eudocia
events.summary: On 7 June 421 Theodosius II married Athenais, daughter of the Athenian pagan sophist Leontius, baptised Eudocia, reportedly chosen by his sister Pulcheria. A poet and later patron of Jerusalem, she became Augusta in 423.
events.debate: Malalas's romantic bride-show tale is late and embroidered.

events.title: Roman-Persian war and the Peace of 422
events.summary: A persecution of Christians under Bahram V and Roman refusal to return fugitives led to war in 421: Ardabur ravaged Arzanene and besieged Nisibis, the Persians besieged Theodosiopolis. The 422 peace bound each side to tolerate the other's religious minority and to build no new forts near the frontier.
scholarship: Greatrex & Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II (2002)
events.debate: The treaty is reconstructed from later references (Procopius, Malchus); the claim of a '100-year peace' is modern shorthand.

events.title: Defeat of Castinus in Baetica
events.summary: The magister militum Castinus, having quarrelled with Bonifatius (who left for Africa), led a Roman army with Gothic federates against the Vandals in Baetica. Betrayed by his Gothic allies, he was routed and lost 20,000 men according to Hydatius, leaving southern Spain to the Vandals.

sides.strength: field army with Gothic federates; commander Castinus
Hasding Vandals and Alans under Gunderic

battle.significance: The last major western offensive in Spain for a generation; it opened the road to Cartagena and Seville and to the sea.

events.title: Death of Honorius; usurpation of Joannes
events.summary: Honorius died of oedema at Ravenna on 15 August 423, after 28 years of nominal rule. Galla Placidia and her children were in exile at Constantinople after a quarrel with him, so the western court proclaimed the senior bureaucrat Joannes, primicerius notariorum, on 20 November.

events.title: Eastern army overthrows Joannes
events.summary: Theodosius II sent Ardabur and his son Aspar to install Valentinian. Ardabur was captured at sea, but Aspar seized Ravenna, guided, Socrates says, by an angel in the form of a shepherd across the marshes. Joannes was taken to Aquileia, mutilated, paraded on an ass in the hippodrome and beheaded. Aetius arrived three days later with a reported 60,000 Huns and had to be bought off.

events.title: Valentinian III proclaimed Augustus at Rome
events.summary: Valentinian III, aged six, was proclaimed Augustus in Rome on 23 October 425 by the eastern master of offices Helion. His mother Galla Placidia governed as regent until about 437, balancing the generals Felix, Bonifatius and Aetius against one another.
events.detail: The price of eastern help was Valentinian's betrothal to Theodosius II's infant daughter Licinia Eudoxia (married 437) and, probably, the cession of western Illyricum to the East.

events.title: Theodosius II founds the Capitolium school
events.summary: A law of 27 February 425 established 31 salaried chairs at the Capitolium in Constantinople: 3 Latin and 5 Greek rhetors, 10 Latin and 10 Greek grammarians, 1 philosopher and 2 jurists, with a ban on private teachers lecturing in public. Greek outnumbering Latin in the rhetoric chairs signals where the eastern court's culture was heading.
events.debate: Calling it a 'university' is anachronistic, but it was the first state-funded teaching body of its kind.

events.title: Vandals and Alans cross to Africa
events.summary: In May 429 Gaiseric led the Vandals and Alans across the Straits of Gibraltar from around Iulia Traducta. Victor of Vita says he counted 80,000 people, including old men, children and slaves, to give an impression of numbers. Within ten years they held Carthage.
events.detail: Procopius claims Bonifatius, comes Africae, invited them in his quarrel with Placidia; this is probably a later story built on his revolt of 427, when Placidia sent armies against him. The Vandals marched some 2,000 km east along the coast, meeting little organised resistance from the Mauretanian provinces. Their ability to ferry tens of thousands across shows access to Spanish shipping, which would later make them the only barbarian naval power.
events.debate: The 80,000 figure is debated as total population vs a symbolic count; Goffart doubts it reflects a census at all. The invitation by Bonifatius is rejected by most (Wijnendaele, Merrills & Miles).
scholarship: Wijnendaele, The Last of the Romans: Bonifatius (2015)
